Record of Karmic Bonds Enduring for Long Distances. Case One: The Story of the Western Sage Dharmamitra, Who Underwent Five Hundred Lifetimes as a Dog.
The Story of the Western Sage Dharmamitra, Who Underwent Five Hundred Lifetimes as a Dog.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
there was a noble bhikṣu named Dharmamitra in the mountains of Kaśmīra.
His talent and wisdom were transcendent, and he was foremost in seated meditation.
At the residence of Maitreya, there were three tiers of caves.
At that time, there were two monks.
Having heard of his supreme reputation from afar, he went to pay him homage.
There he saw the Venerable One wearing tattered robes that were shabby and exposed;
before a hearth in a lower cave, he was kindling a fire for the sake of disciplining his body and mind for the sake of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the two monks asked,
"Where is the Elder Dharmamitra? He replied:
He went to seek him out in that most excellent chamber within the deep cave,
but through his supernormal power, the Venerable One suddenly returned to his own room.
When the two men saw this, they were all filled with doubt and wonder,
saying, "The Great Virtuous One is a holy man whose fame fills Jambudvīpa.
For what reason have you humbled yourself to light a fire for the monks?"
Maitreya said: "My son,
you should now know that I have reflected upon the long duration of suffering within birth and death."
"If it were possible for my head and hands to be set ablaze,
I would do so for the sake of the Sangha;
how much more so for other parts of my body and the kindling of fire."
"What difficulty is there in this?
I recall that in the past,
throughout five hundred lifetimes, I was constantly a dog, suffering from hunger and destitution."
Although many lifetimes have passed, I have been satiated only twice.
Once, I encountered a man by the roadside who was drunk from drinking wine and had vomited;
I met him as I was traveling and obtained one meal of fullness.
Furthermore, he once served as a dog for a poor household.
The husband and wife cooked some gruel and placed it in a vessel;
they then had to go out on business for a short while.
Driven by hunger, I thrust my head into the vessel and ate from it;
having become full, I pulled my head out, but it would not come forth.
People came and saw me.
He gave rise to a great heart of anger and immediately severed my head with a sharp blade.
He thought to himself, "I have undergone this dog's body five hundred times."
Although one may encounter the two types of satiation and thereby lose one's life,
for this reason one should reflect:
birth and death are long-lasting, as one wanders through the five realms of existence.
Wherever one is born, there is no place where suffering is not experienced;
therefore, I now do not shrink from toil and hardship.
"What words are these, that for the sake of the Saṃgha you kindle a fire?

The Holy One of the Western Regions, Śāṇakavāsin, encountered a ghost and a crow, and lamented the long duration of birth and death. This account of the Holy One of the Western Regions, Śāṇakavāsin, encountering a ghost and a crow and lamenting the long duration of birth and death, is recorded in the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (付法藏傳). Formerly, there was the Holy One who transmitted the Dharma, Śāṇakavāsin.
He led his disciples into the city;
upon reaching the gate, he appeared sorrowful and displeased.
After proceeding a short distance further, he saw a crow on the road.
Suddenly he smiled.
His disciples asked him about this in wonder,
and he replied accordingly:
At first, beneath the gate, he saw the son of a hungry ghost,
who was emaciated by hunger and weak with exhaustion, saying to himself:
"My mother gave birth to me."
He entered the city to seek food;
it had been five hundred years since they parted.
Starving, destitute, and impoverished, his life would not last much longer.
Upon meeting his mother,
he related his situation in full.
The mother said,
"I took my leave to enter the city long ago, but I could not obtain any food.
Even if I had obtained a little, the *sātaghna* spirits snatched it away."
Beginning today, I have encountered one person who has spat;
there are no other ghosts nearby.
I am about to give this to you.
However, there are many spirits and deities within the gate who fear being robbed;
therefore, they do not dare to carry it out.
I pray that the Venerable One, through the compassionate shade of your protection, will lead me out of the city.
The tears and saliva he had brought were shared and eaten with his son.
I then asked him, "How long has it been since you were born?"
He replied,
"I have witnessed this city being formed and destroyed seven times.
Hearing those words, I am deeply grieved that birth and death have no end."
For this reason, he frowned and looked distressed and unhappy.
Furthermore, ninety-one kalpas ago,
at that time, I was the son of a householder.
"My supreme aspiration is to leave the household life and grow weary of worldly desires.
If I were to renounce the world, I would surely sever all fetters and become an Arhat;
however, my parents do not permit me to follow my own will."
He was forcibly betrothed to a wife in hopes of securing an heir;
unable to avoid it,
he married and fathered a son.
Furthermore, he sought to leave the household life.
When the son was six years old,
his parents instructed him.
If your father takes leave of me wishing to go forth into the homeless life,
you should embrace his feet and say to him:
"If you abandon me and depart, who will sustain my life?"
"I must first be killed before I may depart.
Seeing my son embrace me, affection arose within me,
and I spoke to him, saying:
"I shall no longer leave the household life for your sake;
because of this son, I am unable to realize the fruit of the Path."
For ninety-one kalpas, they have transmigrated through the five realms of existence;
yet with their bodies of birth and death,
they have never met one another.
Now, with the eye of the Way,
I see him born among crows;
I take pity on his childish ignorance.
It is for this reason that I smile.

Regarding the matter of how the Western Sage, the Pratyekabuddha Revata, once slandered someone for stealing an ox and received retribution: long ago, to the west of the city of the kingdom of Yuezhi, there was a great mountain.
This was the dwelling place of the pratyekabuddha Revata.
Not far from where he ascended into the air,
there was a man who had lost his oxen.
Upon reaching this mountain,
he encountered this pratyekabuddha lighting a fire to dye his robes;
it was due to the power of his past karma.
At that time, the alms bowl transformed into an ox head;
the Dharma robes transformed into ox hide;
and the dyeing liquid transformed into blood.
The dyed dregs transform into flesh;
the firewood transforms into bone.
Since the traces are thus, [the result follows].
He was consequently seized by the owner of the ox and cast into prison;
his disciples searched for him everywhere but could not discover his whereabouts.
From that time on, twelve years passed by in the gradual flow of time.
Later, upon encountering the necessary conditions, he learned that [the teacher] was in prison.
He then went to the king and said, "My teacher is in prison; I pray that Your Majesty will grant him a pardon."
The king asked the jailer whether there were any monks [in prison].
The jailer replied, "There are no monks.
The disciple said to the king, "I pray that you will summon the śramaṇa from within the prison."
When my teacher himself came out,
the prison official immediately called for the pratyekabuddha, who then emerged.
This pratyekabuddha had already been in the prison for a long time.
His hair was long, his robes were tattered, and the appearance of a śramaṇa had vanished.
His disciples prostrated to him and asked,
"Master, why are you here?"
At that time, the Master answered with the aforementioned matters.
The disciple asked again:
"What causes did you create in past lives?"
"Now this has brought me to this state.
The teacher replied,
"In the past, I slandered another for stealing a cow."
This is how it came to pass.

The Monk Huida of the Jin Dynasty Dies and Enters Hell, Along with Accounts of His Violations of the Precepts in Previous Lives. The account of the monk Huida of the Jin dynasty dying and entering hell, including his violations of the precepts in previous lives, is recorded in the *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Omens) and other sources. Huida’s secular surname was Liu, his given name was Sahuo, and he was a native of Lishi in Hexi.
During his time as a householder, he spent long periods in military service;
he had never heard the Buddha’s Dharma,
was skilled with weapons, and took pleasure in hunting.
At the age of thirty-one, he died of a sudden illness.
His body was gentle and supple;
the family did not dare to enshroud him.
Upon reaching the seventh day,
he revived and said:
"At the moment when [my life] was about to end..."
He saw two men binding them and leading them away toward the northwest; as they traveled,
the road grew increasingly steep.
After proceeding a short distance along a level road lined with trees on both sides,
he saw a man standing in the middle of the path holding a bow and wearing a sword at his side.
The two men pointed with their fingers toward the west,
where they saw many houses.
Suddenly, they beheld two śramaṇas.
He said to He, "Do you recognize me? He replied.
He did not know.
The śramaṇa said,
"Now you should take refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha."
Puṇya, as he had been told, gave rise to the thought and followed along with the śramaṇa.
From afar, they saw a city.
It resembles the city of Chang’an, yet its color is extremely black;
it is likely an iron city.
The people seen there are exceedingly tall.
His skin was large and black as lacquer,
and his hair trailed upon the ground.
The śramaṇa said:
These are the ghosts within this hell.
That place is extremely cold;
there are stones of ice that fly about and scatter.
If it strikes the head, the head is severed;
if it strikes the feet, the feet are severed;
if it strikes the arms, the arms are severed.
The two śramaṇas said,
"This is the Hell of Cold Ice. Thereupon,
he reproached himself within and immediately recognized his past lives.
He knew that the two śramaṇas had been his teachers during the time of the Buddha Vipaśyin;
however, when they later sought to become śramaṇas,
they were unable to receive the precepts because they had committed secular offenses.
Although there were Buddhas in the world, he never managed to see one.
From that time until now, he has obtained a human body twice;
in one lifetime, he was born among the Qiang people.
In this life, he was born in the land of Jin.
Next, he saw the Hell of the Mountain of Knives;
he experienced and observed many such places in succession.
Each prison is a distinct realm, not intermingled with one another;
the number of people there is extremely great,
beyond all calculation.
The methods of torture and punishment were roughly consistent with what is described in the sutras.
Suddenly, there appeared a brilliant golden radiance, bright and clear;
within it stood a person approximately twenty feet tall.
His physical marks and secondary characteristics were majestic and beautiful;
his entire body was golden in color.
Those to his left and right said:
This was the Great Being Avalokiteśvara.
All rose to greet him and pay their respects.
There were two śramaṇas whose physical forms closely resembled one another.
Traveling together through the East and West,
Saha completed his prostrations,
and the Bodhisattva preached the Dharma for him in full detail.
He uttered more than a thousand words,
further saying:
"You shall undergo the retribution of suffering through successive kalpas."
"Because you have heard the Dharma in the past, you have given rise to a heart of joy.
Now, having received this light retribution for a single instance, you shall be released.
Since you have attained deliverance and life, you may become a śramaṇa."
Sahuo encountered someone again, who said to him,
"When you were in Xiangyang, why did you kill the deer?"
The deer knelt and replied,
"Another killed the deer;
I merely added the stake."
Furthermore, he did not eat meat;
by what cause did he receive this retribution?
At that moment, he saw the place in Xiangyang where he had shot the deer.
The grasses, trees, mountains, and thickets appeared vividly before his eyes;
the black horses he was riding were all able to speak,
and each testified to the specific year, month, day, and time of the deer's slaughter.
Sahā was terrified and had no reply.
After a short while, a man appeared and impaled him with a forked stake.
Cast into a cauldron of boiling water,
he beheld his own four limbs disintegrate and rot away; then,
a wind blew his body back, gathering it upon the shore of the water.
Suddenly, without his realizing it, his body was restored to its original form.
People spoke to him again, saying,
"You once shot pheasants and also killed geese."
Having spoken thus, he was cast again into the cauldron of boiling water;
as before, his body was boiled and disintegrated.
Only after having undergone this retribution was Saha permitted to depart.
He went into a great city where people lived,
and they said to He:
"You shall undergo this light retribution and then be reborn again.
Supported by the power of this merit, from now on you shall no longer commit transgressions."
He then dispatched people to escort Saha.
From afar, Saha saw his former body and did not wish to return.
Those who were escorting him pushed and pulled him,
and after a long time he finally regained consciousness and was restored to life.
He served the Dharma with diligent devotion and subsequently left the household life. Thereafter,
he attained profound realization through meditation and performed wondrous transformations.
There is a separate biography.

Regarding the matter of the Tang dynasty śramaṇa Daoguang who sought ordination but could not obtain an official name: this account of the Tang dynasty śramaṇa Daoguang seeking ordination but failing to receive an official name has been extracted from the *Xin lu* (New Record) by the monk Daoguang.
He was a native of Bingzhou.
His secular surname was Zhang, and his family tradition was one of quiet withdrawal from worldly affairs.
He felt shame in holding a titled office.
In his youth, he already transcended worldly customs; from an early age, he understood the practice of fasting and purification.
At the age of ten, he took leave of his parents and traveled far and wide in search of the Way.
Thereupon, he shaved his head and wandered as a guest in Guanzhong.
Later, he served under Vinaya Master Daoxuan;
his practice and realization were particularly outstanding. Wheeling through sincerity and reflecting upon it repeatedly, he attained deep insight.
From dawn until dusk, he sought instruction and counsel;
as for his filial care— providing warmth and coolness—
he far surpassed all his peers.
Xuān treated him with both sincere affection and ritual propriety,
providing him with increasingly extensive instruction and guidance.
After several years of diligent study, he eventually became a vessel of great capacity.
However, when the Yonghui era succeeded to the throne, the Emperor took a keen interest in the Buddhist community and repeatedly granted ordinations; yet every time,
due to various circumstances, Sengguang was not included among those selected.
In his heart, he felt constant shame and resentment, harboring perpetual dissatisfaction.
During the Linde era, [the Emperor] proclaimed his virtue through the precepts.
Suddenly, he felt that celestial deities came and went,
engaging him in discussions on the principles of names and reality for several successive months,
tracing back through the teachings of several past Buddhas.
He had thoroughly investigated every detail regarding the times, places, and circumstances of [the Buddha’s] past conduct.
Consequently, he inquired about the scriptural and disciplinary teachings on what is permitted and prohibited, as well as the origins of the sacred sites;
he then composed a comprehensive record in ten fascicles.
Furthermore, during a moment of leisure,
he asked the celestial deity, saying,
"Xuan has a disciple named Daoguang."
His filial piety and love were so pure and profound that he did not know by what karma he had come to be thus.
The spirit said:
Guang and the Vinaya Master were father and son, teacher and disciple,
having already passed through more than three hundred lifetimes together.
It was because their bond of affection and intimacy had endured for so long that this came to pass.
The retribution of past karma and remaining conditions have not yet been exhausted.
He asked again:
"Why did Guang frequently seek ordination?"
In the end, his wishes were not fulfilled.
"What karma has caused this? he asked.
The spirit replied:
Long ago, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha,
when [the protagonist] was serving as the abbot of a monastery,
there was a certain monk.
His observance of the precepts was frequently deficient.
The abbot of the monastery became incensed with him and sent him back to lay life.
Due to this karma, in birth after birth he entered the Way but did not receive the title of an official;
the remaining retribution of this karma has not yet been exhausted.
After Xuān passed away,
Guāng chose his destination between the East and West,
eventually settling in the region north of the River.
In the second year of the Shangyuan era,
the Emperor, for the sake of Empress Xiao-jing,
renovated Baima Temple.
The temple head, Chongyi, exerted every effort in his search.
As Guang’s reputation as a śrāvaka had long been renowned,
he was deemed worthy of this auspicious selection.
Having been granted a name through imperial examination, he entered the palace. Subsequently, as he fell ill,
an imperial edict was issued for him to proceed to Weizhou.
His body has already passed away;
this verifies that the words of the deity are indeed true.
There was also the Chan Master Boliang.
I associated with Master Guang for several years,
frequently receiving his oral teachings which I committed to memory.
When I heard that he had passed away after becoming ill, I was deeply grieved.
Only then did he realize that his karma and destiny were such as this. He recounted the full account to me.

**Record of the Perverse Icchantika:** The Case of Daozhi of Beidu Bao Temple in the Song Dynasty Stealing a Buddha-Image Jewel and Suffering Retribution. Nun Zhītōng (attached to the record of Daozhi). It is not clearly known where she was from. Daozhi, a resident of Beidu Bao Temple in the Northern Song, stole a jewel from a Buddhist image. She subsequently suffered retribution. [The details follow. Nun Zhītōng is appended to the record of Daozhi; her place of origin is unknown.
He left home to become a monk at a young age and resided at Duobao Monastery in the north during the Song dynasty.
He once served as the custodian of the temple halls and pagodas.
He stealthily stole items such as curtains and canopies;
subsequently, he even stole the pearl between the eyebrows of a Buddhist image.
Thereafter, he proceeded to break through the walls.
If it is an external thief,
the monastic community will not be aware of it;
after more than ten days have passed, he will fall ill.
He then saw a strange person strike him with a halberd;
as the assailant came and went, he would cry out in alarm each time,
and blood would flow immediately upon the sound of his voice.
At first, he underwent this twice during the day;
later, it became even more severe, with pricks gradually increasing in number until his entire body was covered in wounds.
His moaning and crying did not cease.
The monks of that temple grew quite suspicious that he had committed a transgression and wished to perform a repentance ritual on his behalf.
At first, when questioned, he still avoided the matter and would not speak;
only after two or three days had passed did he fully recount his circumstances and plead for salvation with tears.
He said, "I am foolish and ignorant, clouded regarding the Way.
I thought there was no suffering like that of the burning pit and the cauldron; thus, losing my right mind, I committed transgressions."
They incur such calamitous cruelty as to undergo torture while alive and suffer the blade and the cauldron after death.
My body is already worn out; I have nothing else to offer but my compassion.
I possess only robes, felt blankets, and sandals, which may perhaps suffice for a single assembly.
Furthermore, you must invite old friends to perform repentance on my behalf.
Formerly, I stole two pearl ornaments from the Buddha image;
one has already been given to an elderly woman.
It can no longer be recovered.
One piece has been pawned for money and is currently in the possession of Chen Zhao.
"Now you may redeem it.
As soon as he finished speaking, he passed away.
Having been redeemed, its appearance was utterly transformed.
They also prepared a vegetarian feast and performed repentance rites.
At first, when the artisans set the jewels in place,
they repeatedly adjusted and rotated them, yet in the end, they could not achieve a harmonious fit.
The assembly of monks again performed prostrations and burned incense before he was finally able to put it on.
More than a year later, his fellow students heard a voice in the air during the darkness of night.
Listen closely; this is the voice of one whose will is set upon the Way.
He says that since his death, he has undergone every kind of agony and suffering.
Otherwise, for many years and kalpas, there would have been no time of release.
Fortunately, by relying on the compassionate pity and protection of the assembly of monks who ransomed me with a pearl,
[I have been saved] from the midst of such bitter cruelty.
At this time, there has been a brief interval;
my gratitude is boundless.
Therefore, I have come for a moment to express my thanks.
Having said this, he ceased speaking;
at that moment, the stench of rotting flesh was indescribable.
When his words ended, the odor gradually subsided.
This was at the end of the Taishi era.
The nun Zhītōng left home to become a monastic in her youth.
He resided at Jianjing Temple in the capital.
His faith was not steadfast.
In the ninth year of the Yuanjia era, the Master died.
She left the monastic life and married Li Xifu of Liang in Wei Commandery as his wife;
they had a son who was six or seven years old when their family fell into extreme poverty.
Having nothing to serve as clothing,
when she became a nun, she took several rolls of plain silk— scriptures such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—
and thoroughly pounded them to clothe her child.
After living there for one year, he fell ill;
he became dazed and suffered from palpitations, with his entire body peeling and rotting as if afflicted by fire sores,
and tiny white worms appeared upon it.
When the sun has risen for a short while,
they suffer with bitter pain and toxic affliction, wailing day and night.
They hear a voice from the air saying:
He tore up a sutra to make clothing for himself and received this severe retribution;
more than ten days later, he died.

The Case of Yan Tong of the Northern Qi Who Stole Money, Was Ashamed When the Image Manifested Itself, Contracted Leprosy, and Fell into the Earth, as recorded in the *Guānzhōng Fēngsú Zhuàn*: Yan Tong was a man of unknown origins from somewhere. He stole money and, feeling ashamed when the [Buddha] image manifested itself, he subsequently contracted leprosy and fell into the ground. This account is found in the *Guānzhōng Fēngsú Zhuàn*. Yan Tong was a person whose native place was unknown.
Although I have entered the gateway of the Way,
my aspirations are largely foolish and vulgar;
I rely solely upon [your] meritorious virtues.
In order to pray for moistening and nourishment,
he once cast a large bronze statue,
yet its halo, pedestal, and attendant figures were all entirely omitted.
Whatever wealth he obtained from alms, he immediately took for himself,
while he made the image pay out its "taxes" as a slave.
After a long period of time had passed, he eventually obtained nothing at all.
The official Tongbian Zhi held up his staff and said to the statue,
"Why does your slave not come out to pay his tax?
I am about to flog him."
Before he had even raised his hand,
he suddenly saw a man two zhang tall,
clad in armor, who came straight forward with glaring eyes and said:
"What reckless wretch dares to treat a Buddha image with such insolence! he cried,
then seized him by the neck and lifted him several feet off the ground,
lashing him with an iron staff.
From head to foot, his entire body was covered in flowing blood;
he cried out in distress, his voice heard both within and beyond the village.
Among the monastics and laypeople who witnessed this, there was none whose heart did not tremble with cold dread.
Beyond ten days, beneath the wounds from the staff,
leprosy sores broke out anew.
They are as large as peaches or apricots;
pus drains and overflows,
leaving the entire body crimson.
It appeared like a blazing fire;
even at a distance of several paces,
the heat reached one's side.
Tong merely cried out and rolled about day and night amidst pus and blood;
after more than a hundred days had passed,
the floor of his room sank down by several feet.

He died thereupon. Regarding the matter of Tang Sili breaking a statue to steal silk and being crushed by a deity: Tang Sili’s family name is not clearly known. He broke a statue to steal its silk and was subsequently crushed by a deity. Tang Sili’s family name is not clearly known.
He was a native of Lantian in Yongzhou.
By nature he was mediocre and shallow, his ambitions being directed solely toward trivial gain;
though he wore the black robes of a monk, he had not yet been permeated by the true transformation.
During the Xianheng era,
he entered the summer retreat at Wuzhen Temple in Langu Valley.
At that time, there were several dozen disciples present, most of whom were highly refined in their practice.
Li Touxing was a hypocrite whose empty boasting always harbored subversive designs.
He then stole the silk from within a statue inside the hall;
several days later, the monks discovered it.
No one knew who had stolen it;
as they interrogated one another in turn, everyone harbored doubts and confusion,
and many felt remorseful, each wishing to flee and disperse.
At that time, the Elder Dharmagupta addressed the assembly, saying:
"It has been heard that this monastery possesses a great many sacred traces.
Now that there is someone who has damaged and broken these images,"
How could the guardian deity of the monastery remain silent?
Within three days, we pray that you will reveal the matter so that the monastic community may find peace.
Having finished speaking,
they each returned to their respective quarters beneath the bell tower and took a nap during the day.
Thereupon, he beheld a great deity dressed in white robes.
He placed the *li* (ceremonial staff) between the bed and the wall,
bowed his head downward, and pressed it down with a stone.
When morning came, the monks could no longer find the *li*.
He went to the room to search for him,
but it was firmly locked and he could not open it despite his efforts.
After one night had passed, his sense of wonder and unease grew even greater.
He then excavated a cave for a door and window,
and saw Li himself sitting upright upon the bed,
with layers of silk from within the statue draped over his body.
They then carried him together to the outside of the gate.
Seeing that his complexion was as black as lacquer and his breath had ceased,
the monks performed a repentance ritual on his behalf.
After a long time, he gradually revived;
he confessed his own sins and evils,
then fled into the night.

It is unknown where it ended. 3. Record of Slighting and Destroying the Teachings of the Dharma. Record of Slighting and Destroying the Teachings of the Dharma, Part Three. The Fivefold Grave Incident of the Venerable Vasubandhu of the Western Regions, who Slandered the Mahāyāna. The Fivefold Grave Incident of the Venerable Vasubandhu of the Western Regions, who Slandered the Mahāyāna. According to the *Xiyu zhuan* (Record of the Western Regions), there was once a śramaṇa from Khotan [who said]: "In the past, there was a master of treatises from the Western Regions..."
His name was Vimalamitra; in the language of Tang, it means "Vimalamitra" (Stainless Friend).
He was a native of Kaśmīra.
He entered the monastic order within the Sarvāstivāda school;
his mastery of the Hīnayāna was so profound that his fame resounded throughout the Five Indias.
As he was returning to his native country on the way, he encountered...
Next was the stupa of the Master of Śāstras Saṃghabhadra.
He patted it and sighed, saying:
"Alas, the Master of Śāstras possessed a refined and lofty character; he upheld and exalted the Great Meaning."
Just as I was about to refute the divergent schools and establish the tenets of our own school,
how is it that my allotted lifespan was not long? I,
Vimalamitra, having humbly inherited the learning of the later generations, [lament this].
At a different time, I admired his righteousness and have cherished his virtue for generations.
Although Vasubandhu has passed away, the traditions of his school still survive;
I shall, to the best of my knowledge, compose various treatises.
"I shall cause the scholars of Jambudvīpa to cease all mention of the Mahāyāna and extinguish the name of Vasubandhu!
Having spoken these words,
his mind fell into a state of frantic madness.
His five tongues protruded and hot blood gushed forth;
knowing his life was surely ending, he composed a letter of repentance, saying:
The Mahāyāna teachings represent the ultimate exposition within the Buddha-dharma.
Their terminology and flavor are transcended, and their principles and doctrines are profound and mysterious.
To treat them with levity and, out of ignorance, to refute those who have gone before is a grave error.
The retribution of cause and effect is as clear as the light of day; it is only right that one should extinguish the self.
I venture to inform the students: the mirror of this truth lies herein.
Each of you should guard your resolve and harbor no doubts.
Immediately the great earth shook and his life came to an end.
At the very spot where he died, the ground subsided to form a pit.
At that time, there was an arhat.

Regarding the account of how Bo-da, a temple attendant within the borders of Fenzhou during the Tang dynasty, died and was reborn as a temple ox: according to the *Xin lu* (New Record), this occurred during the Zhenguan era.
Within a monastery in the borders of Fenzhou,

they followed several dozen paces behind a herd of cattle.

it immediately turned its head back toward the assembly of monks.
The monks said,
"It is mostly Boda," and he then spoke these words:
"If you are truly he, come forth into the midst of the assembly.
At these words, the ox came immediately,
bowing its head to the ground.
Tears flowed from his eyes.
The assembly of monks then patted his head,
and he wept in response to them.
He performed repentance rites and administered the precepts for him.
In the nineteenth year, Emperor Taizong launched a military expedition against Liaodong.
The Vice Minister of the Left, Yuwen Jie,
was ordered to requisition oxen from various prefectures to provide for the army's provisions.

This ox alone remained defiant and obstinate, refusing to come out.

The ox emerged at the sound of his voice;

Yuwen Jie was greatly astonished and departed.

The Case of the Monk Jueyong of Konghui Temple in Yizhou, Tang China, Who Died of Suffering After Using Temple Funds to Carve His Forehead. Regarding the case of the monk Jueyong of Konghui Temple in Yizhou, Tang China, who died of agony after using temple funds to carve his forehead: the new records state that the clan name and surname of the monk Jue are unknown.
In his early years, he left home to dwell at Kōe-ji Temple.

however, his awakening ambition was such that he delighted in peering into others' affairs.

when his turn came to oversee the affairs of the community,

He never felt shame or regret.
Later, he suddenly stripped off his clothes;
standing naked, his hands were bound behind his back.
He wailed and cried out loudly,

Jue said: "I have now manifested this body and entered hell.
There is someone in the air holding a chisel."
He bored large holes in my forehead, the back of my head, and my back;
within these cavities were coins.

numbering either a thousand or a hundred,

It enters through the opening on the back and exits through the mouth;
or it enters through the forehead and exits through the brain, or enters through the brain and exits through the forehead.
When the money was returned,

he wished to perform repentance and seek forgiveness.

his breath was gasping and his piteous cries were agonizing.

prior to this, he had felt as though he were about to vomit blood.

"Why have you fed the fruits of the monastery to your relatives?
Having said this, he vanished.
This occurred regularly for the space of a month.
